senses.definition: A coil or loop of something, especially twine, yarn, or rope.
examples:
1681, E.R., The Experienced Farrier, London, p. 307,
[…] the best thing of all to stop bleeding at the Nose, is to take a Hank of Coventry-blew thread, and hang it cross a stick, and set one end of it on fire […] and let him receive the smoak up his Nostrils […]

quotes.text: Cotton twist is spun here of 130 hanks to the pound. Each hank is 840 yards long […]
quotes.reference: 1796, Thomas Pennant, “History of Holywell Parish,”, in The History of the Parishes of Whiteford, and Holywell, London: B. and J. White, page 217:

quotes.text: […] her hair was as straight as a hank of cotton.
quotes.reference: 1859, George Eliot, chapter 9, in Adam Bede, volume 1, Edinburgh: William Blackwood, page 181:

quotes.text: The past year or two had brought knitting-needles into countenance for men, and he saw no reason why he should not put a few hanks of yarn into shape useful for himself.
quotes.reference: 1919, Henry Blake Fuller, chapter 14, in Bertram Cope’s Year, Chicago: R.F. Seymour, page 131:

quotes.text: He found a hank of clothesline on a counter.
quotes.reference: 1957, Nevil Shute, chapter 9, in On the Beach, New York: William Morrow:

senses.definition: (nautical) A ring or shackle that secures a staysail to its stay and allows the sail to glide smoothly up and down.
A rope or withe for fastening a gate.

quotes.text: Seldom doth a man fall into a Preſumptuous Sin, but vvhere the Devil hath got ſuch a hanke over him, […]
quotes.reference: 1636 July (date delivered), Robert Sanderson, “[Ad Aulam.] Sermon IV. Beuvoyr, July 1636”, in XXXIV Sermons. […], 5th edition, London: […] [A. Clark] for A. Seil, and are to be sold by G. Sawbridge, […], published 1671, →OCLC, paragraph 43, page 59:

senses.definition: (wrestling) A throw in which a wrestler turns his left side to his opponent, twines his left leg about his opponent's right leg from the inside, and throws him backward.
(transitive, UK, dialect) To fasten with a rope, as a gate.

quotes.text: where stood a fyne howse newly built and vaulted, over wheron her armes was sett and hanked with tapestrye
